$schema_note: User-visible product improvements, newest first. Feeds the pipeline's What's-new card and the homepage footer's latest-improvement stamp — one source, both surfaces (the homepage must match the real site). Keep entries honest, dated, and user-phrased; trim to ~12.

entries.title: Twenty-six more metro areas get their own live figures
entries.blurb: A deal in Pittsburgh, Phoenix, Denver, Nashville, Charlotte, Austin, Houston, Minneapolis, San Diego, Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Raleigh, Salt Lake City, San Antonio, Sacramento, Columbus, Indianapolis, Kansas City, St. Louis, Cincinnati, Jacksonville, the Inland Empire, Detroit, Portland or Cleveland now reads the metro area's own published figures — unemployment, payrolls and the five sectors, permits with the single-family split, house prices, the survey's rental vacancy with its margin, Zillow's asking rents and Realtor.com's for-sale market — on the market check, the deal page, the report and the workbook, said as the metro's, where it read its state's before. These markets have no research brief, and every header says so.

entries.title: A deal anywhere in the country gets live figures: its state's own
entries.blurb: The market check and the deal page read a covered metro's published figures; a deal in Pittsburgh, Phoenix or Nashville got none. Now a deal outside the tracked metros reads its state's own series — unemployment, payrolls by sector, permits with the single-family split, house prices and the survey's annual rental vacancy — pulled every weekday from FRED under one pattern a state, and every sentence says the figure is the state's rather than any metro's. The demand and supply pictures, the since-this-screen moves and the model's vacancy check all draw from the same rows.

entries.title: The insurance line gets a published figure
entries.blurb: Insurance is the expense that reprices hardest and gets read least: a memorandum's premium is the seller's expiring policy. The BLS's index of commercial property insurance premiums (commercial multiple peril, the policy a building carries) now rides with the other feeds — against a year ago on the rates strip's inflation fold, on every operating deal's market check as the nation's carriers rather than this building's quote, in the market check's instructions as what the insurance line is checked against, and in the model's expense-growth check beside consumer prices, shown and never averaged into them.

entries.title: The supply side beside the demand side: the apartments each metro is permitting
entries.blurb: Every covered market now shows the units it permitted in buildings of two or more over the last twelve months against the twelve before — the pipeline an apartment underwrite competes with — as one stacked bar a year under the jobs picture, single-family beside it, both counts linked to their series. FRED publishes no multi-unit permit series for a metro, so the figure is the total less the single-family series and the page says so. The market check's permits line carries the same split with its own figure, and a rental-housing deal's page and the demo say it in one line under the demand bars.

entries.title: The demo shows the sample market's demand side, live
entries.blurb: The demo's market section — the one page a visitor reads without signing in — now draws the Philadelphia area's payrolls by sector against a year ago, off the same rows a screened deal's market section reads today: all payrolls first, then the five sectors that fill each kind of building, dated, each figure linked to its series. The sample is an apartment building, so nothing is singled out; a screened office, warehouse, store or hotel gets its own sector drawn full, and the sentence under the bars is the deal's own kind's — a storage or land deal is never called rental housing. A read that fails leaves the card out rather than something stale on the page.

entries.title: The deal page draws the demand side of its market
entries.blurb: Under the market check's folded figures, a deal in a covered market now carries a picture of the demand side: the metro area's payrolls by sector against a year ago — all payrolls first, then the five sectors that fill each kind of building — read today from the same rows the market brief draws, with the sector that fills this building's kind drawn full and the others faded. An office reads professional and business services, a warehouse transportation and warehousing, a store retail trade, a hotel leisure and hospitality; rental housing singles nothing out. A sector whose figure has stopped updating is kept and named rather than dropped, and every figure links to its series.

entries.title: The model's vacancy and exit cap, set against the metro's own sector tracker
entries.blurb: The assumptions card under the debt sizer read a commercial deal's vacancy against nothing, because the Census survey counts rental housing and nothing else. The research tracker behind the market brief — each covered metro's office, industrial, retail and apartment vacancy as the houses print it, with the cap range where one is tracked — now rides beside the feeds: an office, a warehouse or a store has its stabilized vacancy set against the tracker's band for its metro, dated and sourced as the quarterly print it is; an apartment deal's survey check carries the tracker's read beside the Census figure, never in its place; and where the tracker has a cap range, the exit cap is set against it as well as against today's 10-year, with an exit under the range's low end named as cap compression on top of the spread. The deal page, the report and the workbook read it through the same one function.

entries.title: Each metro's payrolls by sector, and the one sector a deal reads
entries.blurb: A metro's jobs figure has been one number — all payrolls against a year ago — which is the right figure for an apartment and a blunt one for anything else: an office fills with professional and business services, a warehouse with transportation and warehousing, a store with retail trade, a hotel with leisure and hospitality, a clinic with education and health. Seventy more series from the BLS's state-and-area employment now ride in every weekday pull, five sectors for each of the fourteen metro areas, every id printed by the runner before it was trusted. On the market brief they are one picture under the metro's tiles — signed bars from a centre line, beside all payrolls, each linked to its series — and each commercial sector's own line under its fundamentals. A screen of a deal in a covered market is handed the one sector that fills its kind of building, dated and named as the metro area's, so a lease-up or absorption claim is checked against the payrolls that would have to fill it; rental housing keeps reading all payrolls, and a class no one sector fills reads none rather than a guess. And each sector page ranks the covered markets by that sector's payrolls under its vacancy leaderboard — where the demand for the space is growing, beside where the space is tight, fastest first, with a suburb reading its metro area's figure and saying so. The market page's board now has a twin over the demand side: every metro area against every sector's payroll growth, shaded within each column so office-using jobs compare to office-using jobs, with a stopped series shown with its date rather than ranked.

entries.title: The rents each kind of commercial lessor charges, from the BLS
entries.blurb: An apartment deal has had the metro's own rents to read its growth against — Zillow's asking rents and the rent sitting tenants pay — while an office, a shop, a warehouse or a storage facility had nothing of its own kind. Five more series from the BLS's producer price indexes now ride on the rates strip and into the deal: the rents lessors of professional and office buildings, shopping centers and retail stores, and manufacturing and industrial buildings charge, what self-storage operators charge, and the aggregate for lessors of nonresidential buildings, each against a year ago. A commercial deal's rent growth is set against the index of its own kind of lessor, said as the nation's figure and never the metro's, in the model's assumption check and in the market check's brief; lodging and licensed care, which sell nights and care rather than leases, read none. Every id was printed by the runner before it was trusted, and each commercial sector's line on the market brief now carries the nation's figure under the metro's tracker fundamentals, said as the nation's.

entries.title: The model's assumptions, set against the published figures
entries.blurb: The screening model runs on four numbers that decide its return more than any others — rent growth, expense growth, stabilized vacancy and the exit cap — and two of them start as flat defaults on every deal. A new card under the debt sizer sets each against the published figure that speaks to it: rent growth against the metro's asking rents from Zillow and the rent its sitting tenants pay from the BLS, expense growth against consumer prices, vacancy against the Census survey's metro figure inside its margin of error, and the exit cap's spread over today's 10-year Treasury beside the going-in cap's, so an exit that assumes cap compression is named as one. Every figure is dated with its publisher, nothing is a verdict — a trailing year is what an assumption is being asked to beat, not a forecast — and a figure is only ever set against an assumption of its own kind: an office is never read against apartment rents. The full report prints the same read under its sensitivity grids, and the Excel model carries it as a Market Read tab beside its Assumptions — one row a published figure, the value raw — so the document and the workbook say what the page says.

entries.title: The sample screen's leverage check reads the week's survey
entries.blurb: The sample screen's leverage check compared the sample's cap with a 30-year mortgage survey figure checked in on August 20 — so the one page a visitor reads without signing in showed a benchmark five weeks old as if it were the week's. It now reads the survey the rates pull writes every week, dated and named as FRED's series, falls back to the checked-in snapshot only where the table has nothing and says so, and prints the cap's spread over today's 10-year Treasury beside it, the way a deal page does. The deal page and the compare table read the same survey through the same cached read, so no two surfaces can print a different benchmark for one day, and a survey the pull has stopped writing is shown as stale beside its date rather than swapped for something older.

entries.title: The leverage check reads today's curve
entries.blurb: The deal page's leverage check compared the going-in cap with the 30-year mortgage survey and nothing else — an owner-occupier rate, which is why it only ever said which way the spread pointed. It now also says the cap's spread over the 10-year Treasury as published that morning, the figure every buyer and lender quotes a cap against, with its date and no verdict, and reads leverage against the rate the model itself was seeded with — today's index plus a screening spread for the asset class — naming both halves so the assumption is in the open. The compare table gets the same 10-year spread as a signed row beside its leverage row, so four deals can be read against one day's curve.

entries.title: The figures follow the check into the verdict and the report
entries.blurb: The published figures the market check reads — the metro's rents, vacancy and permits, and the debt market's 10-year and lending standards — now reach the verdict as their own dated section, with the synthesizer told to name a figure and its date as the source of a screen range or a next step rather than a rule of thumb. The full report prints them under the market checks, and a shared screen's market read says how many were read, for which metro, on which day. A check that read none leaves all three as they were.

entries.title: The market check reads the debt market too
entries.blurb: Beside the metro's rents, vacancy and permits, the market check is now handed the capital side of the deal, national and dated: the 10-year Treasury that the exit cap and the permanent quote key off, what banks say about their own lending standards for this kind of loan — multifamily for rental housing, nonresidential for everything else, construction for a plan — as the Fed's quarterly survey reports it, CRE delinquency at commercial banks, and bank CRE lending against a year ago. The check is asked to test the exit cap and the debt assumptions against them and cite the figure with its date, and the figures it read fold open on the deal page with the rest.

entries.title: Every feed, judged on its own cadence
entries.blurb: The data-health page now shows what each feed last wrote — FRED's daily, weekly, monthly and quarterly series apart, the metro series, the BLS rent index, the Census survey, Zillow and Realtor.com — with the newest observation, its age, and whether every series in it is current for its own cadence, the stale ones named. The nightly steward could only ask whether the rates table as a whole had anything newer than five days, which a dead monthly pull passes as long as the Treasury curve keeps arriving; this cannot be fooled that way. A feed with no rows says no rows, never current.

entries.title: What moved since the screen
entries.blurb: A screen is a snapshot, and a deal page is opened for weeks after it ran. The market check now remembers the figures it read as values, not only as sentences, and a deal page opened later reads the same metro's figures today and says what moved since the check ran — the asking rent up 1.1% to $2,335, the metro's unemployment up 0.4 of a point, the for-sale market twelve places hotter — each in its own unit. It keeps three things apart that should never read the same: a figure that moved, a figure with a newer observation that did not move, and a figure its publisher has not updated since the screen.

entries.title: The market check reads this month's figures for the metro
entries.blurb: The screen's market check reasoned from rules of thumb alone, and said so, while the market brief beside it showed the metro's published figures. For a deal inside a covered market the check is now handed those same figures, each dated and with its publisher — this month's asking rents from Zillow, the rent sitting tenants are paying from the BLS, the metro's rental vacancy with its margin of error from the Census survey, a year of building permits, payrolls and house prices from FRED, and the for-sale market from Realtor.com — and told to check the memorandum's assumptions against the figure where one answers, to cite it with its date, and to say a metro figure is the metro's rather than the submarket's. The figures it read are stored with the result and fold open under the check on the deal page, so the evidence is never hidden. Outside the covered markets the check reasons as it always did.

entries.title: The model's interest rate is today's, not a placeholder
entries.blurb: Every deal's screening model ran on a flat 6.00% all-in rate, whatever the market was doing that day, and the deal page's debt sizer and construction panel on flat figures of their own. The rate now starts the way a lender quotes one: the Treasury tenor nearest the hold — the 5-year on a five-year hold — as published on FRED that morning, plus a screening spread for the asset class, with the note naming both halves and the date ("5-yr Treasury 4.78% (FRED, Sep 17, 2026) + 200 bps multifamily spread, a screening default — enter your quote"). The construction loan starts from 30-day average SOFR plus a construction spread. The deal page, the Excel model, the report and the assumption bridge all read the same figure, so no two of them print a different rate for one deal on one day; a loan the documents state still wins, because a quote beats a benchmark; and on a day the table cannot be trusted the old placeholder stays, with a note that never claims the market was consulted.

entries.title: Each metro area's own rental vacancy, with its margin of error
entries.blurb: Every covered market's live panel now carries the Housing Vacancy Survey's own quarterly rental vacancy rate for the metro area — the figure the Census Bureau publishes only as a spreadsheet, for the 75 largest metros — beside the region's rate it already showed. It comes with the survey's margin of error printed under it, because a sample's figure for one metro is wide (Richmond's ±5 points on a 7% rate) and a rate shown without its margin reads as more than it is: a quarter's move inside the margin is noise, and the region's figure beside it is the steadier one. Pulled each quarter after the survey's release, matched by the metro area's name and checked from the runner before it was trusted.

entries.title: How hot the for-sale market is, against the country
entries.blurb: Each market's for-sale line now carries Realtor.com's hotness rank — where the metro sits among the 300 largest by how many buyers look at each listing and how fast homes sell, each against the U.S. — with the rank it held the same month a year earlier, so the move on the year is said the right way round (a smaller number is hotter), and the two parts in plain units: listing views per property as a share above or below the U.S., days on market as days faster or slower. A hot for-sale market is one where buyers compete for homes, and the ones who lose out keep renting — the demand side an apartment underwrite is quietly assuming. Read from Realtor.com's own history file, credited as its terms require.

entries.title: Chicago at sunrise
entries.blurb: Chicago's photograph — on its market brief and in the markets gallery — was a soft daytime strip of the skyline. It is now the whole skyline at first light across the water, every tower lit under a sky going blue: found by a Chicago-only search of Wikimedia Commons run from the site's own build runner, chosen by eye from a contact sheet of twenty-six candidates, and credited to its photographer, NorbertNagel, under CC BY-SA 4.0 as the licence requires. Philadelphia, Jersey City, New York and Boston were looked at on the same day and kept: each was already the strongest frame on its sheet.

entries.title: A mandate stated in units, keys or pads
entries.blurb: The buy box's size band was square feet only, and an apartment buyer's mandate is not — it is "100 to 400 units". The box now takes a count band beside the square-feet one, and every screened deal is checked against it in its own noun: "Keys" on a hotel, "Pads" on a manufactured-housing community, "Beds" on a student deal, read from the memorandum's own count row. A memorandum that states its unit count and never its area — most apartment decks — is judged on the count rather than parked on a blank, and the fit score's size dimension folds the two bands the way the checks do: a miss on either is a miss, a near-miss on either earns partial credit. The public sample's mandate carries one now, so the demo's buy-box tab shows the check at 248 units.

entries.title: Each market's rental vacancy, from the Census region it sits in
entries.blurb: Every covered market's live panel now carries a rental vacancy rate — the Census Bureau's Housing Vacancy Survey, quarterly, pulled through FRED every weekday. The survey publishes it for the four Census regions and never for a metro, so the tile carries the region's figure and says so in its label ("Rental vacancy · South Census region") rather than passing a region's number off as a city's; the South sits near 9.5% where the West is near 5.3%, which is the spread an underwriter's vacancy assumption should at least know about. Each of the four series was printed from the runner with its own title before it was trusted.

entries.title: The model's area, when the memorandum states none
entries.blurb: An apartment memorandum often states its unit count and never its square footage. The Excel model used to run its per-square-foot lines on a flat 100,000 SF in that case — a placeholder marked as an assumption, but a made-up figure all the same. It now runs on the unit count times the deal type's typical size (850 SF an apartment, 550 a hotel key, 350 a student bed), and the Sources column says exactly that — "248 units × 850 SF typical — enter the rentable SF" — so the number is yours to correct rather than one to discover. Only a deal with no count at all still falls to the placeholder.

entries.title: The buy box, the model and the comps in the deal's words
entries.blurb: The buy box now offers every deal type the site files, so a hotel or a storage buyer can set a mandate, and its basis check reads "Basis / key" on a hotel and "Basis / pad" on a park against the figure the memorandum actually quotes. The Excel model's per-unit rows say "Price / Key" and "Year-1 Rent / Pad / Month" in the deal's own noun, the comps page's bars and the report's captions do the same, and each of the newly filed deal types asks for its own facts — a net lease's tenant credit and rent bumps, a medical office's campus, a data center's committed power, a student deal's pre-leasing.

entries.title: Every deal in its own words
entries.blurb: A hotel is counted in keys and priced per key, a manufactured-housing community in pads, a student deal in beds, a site in acres — and the screen now says so everywhere: the deal page's header and size, the memo and the report, the Excel model's cover, the comp memories, the plan's all-in basis, the manual deal form and the challenger all read one table of each deal type's words. Seven more types can be filed: net lease, medical office, mixed-use, student housing, senior housing, data center and parking. An office, a hotel or a storage facility is no longer told the city's rent-control rules cover it, a development's land cost is no longer labelled a price beside a cap it does not have, and the challenger grills each type on its own traps — RevPAR's two levers and the fee stack on a hotel, street rate against in-place on storage, the entitlement odds and the carry on land, dark value on a net lease — instead of asking every building about loss-to-lease.

entries.title: A picture of each building, from its own memorandum
entries.blurb: Every deal on the signed-in site now opens on a photograph of its building: the cover picture out of the offering memorandum you uploaded, lifted from the file the first time the deal is opened, sized once for the deal page and again for the pipeline's thumbnail, and credited to the memorandum. Where a memorandum carries no photograph — a scanned deck, a text-only teaser — the overhead stays, as before, and the deal page's Add photo button takes a picture of your own (Replace photo, once there is one). A reissued memorandum drops the picture taken from the old one; a picture you added survives it. The picture is never fetched from a listing portal or an image search: the memorandum's cover was sent to you to evaluate the deal, which is exactly this use, and a portal's photograph is under that portal's terms. The sample deal keeps its overhead.

entries.title: The for-sale market, under the rent
entries.blurb: Each market's brief now carries this month's for-sale market from Realtor.com's inventory file: the median list price, the active listings and the median days on market, each against a year ago. The rent lines above it say what a renter pays and what a home costs in years of it; this says the flow behind that price — a market where listings pile up and sit longer is loosening, and a loosening market is one a renter can buy into, while fewer and faster keeps them renting. The call is made only when both flow figures agree and never from the price alone, and the line says plainly that a list price is what sellers are asking, not what buyers paid. Matched by CBSA code and checked by name from the runner before it was trusted; Realtor.com's condition for use is attribution, and the line carries it.

entries.title: The apartment asking rent, and what a home costs in years of it
entries.blurb: Zillow's all-homes asking rent runs over houses, condos and apartments together, so in a market of dear houses it sits well above what an apartment actually lets for. Each market's brief now shows the same index over apartment listings alone — the figure an apartment underwrite should be reading — as a third bar beside the all-homes rent and the fair market rent HUD pays, with the gap said. And beside it the typical home value, said against a year of asking rent as the price-to-rent ratio in years, which is the arithmetic that keeps a renter renting. Both come from two more of Zillow's monthly files, read by the same pull and verified from the runner before they were trusted; a figure the pull does not have is simply absent, never a zero.

entries.title: Each market's rent index, beside its asking rent
entries.blurb: Every covered market's brief now carries the CPI's rent of primary residence against a year ago — what sitting tenants pay across the area's leases — drawn on the same panel as its unemployment, jobs, permits and house prices, and read against the asking rent above it, which is this month's new leases. The two are different numbers about different tenants, and an underwrite needs both: a rent roll grows at the first, a vacant unit re-lets at the second. Eight markets' figures come from FRED. Washington's, Baltimore's and Los Angeles's come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics directly, because FRED does not carry the areas the BLS redrew in 2018 — and the tile, the heading and the note all say so, since a figure is never credited to a source that does not publish it. Richmond and Hampton Roads have no CPI area of their own, and a region's figure is not a metro's, so their panel simply has no such tile.

entries.title: Los Angeles opens on the mountains, Dallas on its green tower
entries.blurb: Los Angeles's opening picture was a tight cluster of downtown towers under a blue sky — sharp, and it could have been any city. It is now downtown against the snow on the San Gabriels, the view the city is known by. Dallas's was a hazy aerial from a plane window; it is now downtown at dusk with the green outline of Bank of America Plaza and Reunion Tower behind it. Finding the Dallas picture took a change to the search itself: a run for one market now checks four times as many files as a run for all eighteen, because the narrow run is the one that wants depth. San Francisco, Seattle, Miami and Atlanta keep their pictures, each the best on its sheet. Montgomery County keeps its overhead: two searches found an aerial, an interstate and a category of berries, and a suburb shaped by its land is more honestly photographed from above.

entries.title: Four markets get the photograph they are known by
entries.blurb: Washington's opening picture is no longer an overhead of the Mall but the Lincoln Memorial and Memorial Bridge seen from Arlington, at ground level. Richmond's soft 1,600-pixel skyline became a sharp 5,400-pixel one. Prince George's County, which had kept an aerial on the reasoning that a suburb has no skyline, now opens on the picture it is actually known by — the Capital Wheel at National Harbor at dusk. And Norfolk's file turned out to be a street corner at dusk, a hotel and a garage, so it became the same photographer's daytime waterfront from the Elizabeth River. The change in method is the point: the search that finds candidates prints a file's name, author and size, and none of that says whether a photograph is any good, so it now also saves small copies of every candidate to a contact sheet the site's own tooling can look at. A picture is chosen by eye and still credited from what Wikimedia Commons returned, never from memory. Baltimore's harbour panorama and Rosslyn across the Potomac stayed: their alternatives were handsome aerials, and an aerial is the thing being replaced.

entries.title: What landlords are asking, against what HUD pays
entries.blurb: Each covered market's brief now shows this month's asking rent from Zillow's Observed Rent Index — all home types, refreshed monthly, with its change from a year ago and Zillow's credit — drawn on one scale against the two-bedroom fair market rent HUD pays, with the gap said in words. They are different numbers about different things: the fair market rent is set once a year from survey data two years old by the time it applies, the asking rent is this month's listings before concessions, and an underwrite that mistakes either for the other is wrong in a known direction. A suburb that shares its metro area's figure says so. Pulled on the 20th of each month from Zillow Research's public file; the file's shape and every metro's name in it were checked from the runner before a number was trusted.

entries.title: Each market's own figures, live
entries.blurb: Every covered market's brief now carries the four things FRED publishes for it that a screen actually turns on, pulled every weekday and dated: the metro's unemployment rate, its nonfarm payrolls against a year ago, a year of building permits, and the FHFA house price index against a year ago — each with its recent path and a link to its series. Two rules do the work. A metro's permits arrive as one month's count, not seasonally adjusted, so a month is mostly the season; the panel sums the trailing twelve and sets them against the twelve before, and says nothing rather than scaling up a partial year. And borrowed is said: a suburb has its own unemployment rate and nothing else at this cadence, so where the figure is the metro area's the tile wears the area's name and the note says so — passing an MSA figure off as a county's flatters whichever county is weaker. Every one of the fifty-eight ids was verified from the runner against FRED's own title before it was trusted, which is how the table learned that the Richmond prefix nobody would guess is RICH051, that Boston's obvious unemployment series is the discontinued NECTA one, and that the Washington and Atlanta house price series stopped at 2024 Q4 under the new delineations — so those two tiles are left out rather than shown stale.

entries.title: Every market figure on the site is today's
entries.blurb: The rates strip across the top of the calculators, and at the foot of the market page, used to carry four figures. It now carries forty-six, every one pulled from FRED each weekday and dated: the whole Treasury curve from one month to thirty years, drawn as a line — today solid, a week earlier dashed — with the slope named, because the shape of the curve is a fact you read from a picture and cannot read from eleven tiles; SOFR, its 30-day average, fed funds and prime beside it; and, folded into groups whose summary line already carries the headline figures, the credit spreads, the two mortgage surveys, bank CRE lending and the net share of banks tightening on construction, multifamily and nonresidential loans, inflation and the cost of building (the construction-materials index is running 10% above a year ago), jobs and output, and the multifamily supply pipeline — starts, permits and completions in buildings of five units or more. Every figure links to its series and every tile draws its recent path. Two rules did not change. A benchmark is not a quote, so only a rate a loan document names can pre-fill a field — and the prepayment card now starts from the Treasury tenor nearest its remaining term, the 2-year, rather than the 10-year that would flatter the penalty. And stale is judged per series, because a quarterly figure five months old is current and a daily one a week old is broken. One rule is new: every series id was verified from the runner against FRED's own title before it was trusted, which caught the first list naming a credit-card series as a commercial real estate one. Cap rates have no free daily source, so they stay dated research and say so.

entries.title: The entitlement clock
entries.blurb: The land-residual card solves what the dirt is worth once it is entitled. The zoning card says what the code allows. This is the twelve to thirty-six months in between — the rezoning, the site plan, the permits — which a development pro forma covers as month zero. THE CARRY RUNS ON THE LAND AND NOBODY BUDGETS IT: a pro forma has one line called "land" and it is the purchase price, so twenty-four months at 9% on a $6,000,000 site with $60,000 a year of taxes on the dirt is $1,248,600 before a shovel moves — 20.8% on top of the basis, $52,025 a month against any delay, and invisible because there is no line for it. AN OPTION IS INSURANCE AND ITS PRICE HAS A CLOSED FORM. Set the two paths against each other and everything about the finished building cancels; what is left is the carry you avoid plus the probability-weighted loss on land you would be left holding. Read the identity the other way and it says something exact: where the land is worth what you paid whatever happens, the option is worth precisely the carry, at any odds. The consultants and engineers pursuing the approval are paid on both paths, so they cancel out of the break-even — charging them against the option is the same error the hold-or-sell card prices on selling costs. THE RISK IS A PROBABILITY, NOT A CONTINGENCY: approved the seeded site is worth $1,801,400 and that is the figure a deck shows; across both branches the expectation is $1,590,000 lower, which no contingency percentage describes. And on this deal there is no crossing at all — the quoted fee sits under the carry it replaces, so the option wins at every probability, certainty included. That is why land is optioned rather than bought. One more thing the term sheet settles in a single word: an applicable fee credits against the price on exercise, so it is only spent when the deal dies, and its break-even is far higher — running away entirely as approval nears certainty, which is why nobody grants one.

entries.title: The swap, and getting out of one
entries.blurb: The rate-cap card prices the instrument a bridge lender REQUIRES. This is the one every borrower who calls itself hedged actually has, and it behaves nothing like the other. A CAP IS AN OPTION AND A SWAP IS AN OBLIGATION: a cap costs a premium and pays only when rates rise, so its worst case is the premium; a swap costs nothing at the outset and settles both ways, so its worst case is unbounded and lands on the side nobody stress-tests — rates FALLING. Swapped at 4.50% against a 3.00% market, the seeded $20,000,000 is $845,849 under water. Drawn across a range of market rates the position is a straight line through the strike with NO FLAT STRETCH anywhere; a cap would be flat across the whole left half, and that shape is the difference between the two instruments. THE MARK-TO-MARKET IS THE BREAKAGE COST, and it is what makes a hedged building hard to sell: terminating means writing that cheque at closing on top of everything else. Which is exactly the exit problem yield maintenance creates on a fixed-rate loan, IN THE SAME RATE DIRECTION — so floating-plus-swap, chosen over fixed for its flexibility, has none. Two more things the term sheet does not say. The swap fixes the INDEX and the lender spread rides on top, so a 4.50% swap on SOFR plus 250 is a 7.00% loan and the struck rate is never the coupon. And the notional has to follow the balance: flat against an amortising loan it ends $654,607 over the debt, and a swap that outlasts the loan is a naked rate position settling in cash against a building with no debt on it — the larger number, and the one nobody models, because the loan is gone by then and so is the spreadsheet.

entries.title: The comp adjustment grid
entries.blurb: Three to six sales, adjusted to the subject. Every analyst does this, most of them in a corner of a spreadsheet, and it is the one calculation here whose METHOD is argued over rather than its inputs — while the argument everybody has is worth a rounding error and two things nobody argues about are worth millions. THE ADJUSTMENT IS APPLIED TO THE COMP, so a comp in a worse location than the subject is adjusted UP: it would have sold for more if it were the subject. "The comp is worse, so subtract" feels right and is backwards, and getting it backwards costs roughly twice the adjustment — $2,524,284 on the seeded grid, a ninth of the deal. It does not shade the answer, it REVERSES it: read correctly the 2,000,000 ask is defensible; read backwards the same five sales make it look 11.4% rich and the deal gets passed on. THE TIME ADJUSTMENT COMES FIRST AND IS THE ONE LEFT OUT — a sale twenty-six months old in a six percent market is 13.5% behind before anything about the building is considered, and leaving it out, as a grid of "recent" comps invites, is worth $743,844 against $10,668 for the sequential-versus-additive argument. Seventy times over. GROSS ADJUSTMENT MEASURES COMPARABILITY AND NET DOES NOT: a comp adjusted +15% for location and −15% for size nets to zero, which reads as a perfect comparable and is thirty percent judgement. And the reconciliation is weighted by the inverse of that gross rather than averaged, floored so a one-percent comp is not treated as twice a two-percent one. Paste the grid; a CSV whose figures also carry thousands marks is handed back rather than guessed at.

entries.title: Every card hammered at its edges
entries.blurb: Forty-five calculations, each written against a realistic deal and tested on one. This round did the opposite: every one of the newest modules was fed zeros, negatives, and figures far past the plausible, and anything that came back non-finite, negatively zero or simply absurd was flagged. The arithmetic itself held — not one infinity or NaN anywhere — but four cards were reporting figures that read as answers and were not. The renovation program at a 1% turnover said the program took a hundred years, then drew thirty bars covering sixty of two hundred doors and printed a 42% return off that truncation: three figures, none describing the same program. It now names the pace as a pace rather than a plan and reports no return at all. A renovation invoice at or below the make-ready it displaces has no incremental cost, so there is no return on cost to state — it says to check the two figures instead. A storage concession longer than the average tenancy was costing more than a hundred percent of the rent; the tenant simply never pays, and the cost of that is all of it. And the fee-drag card dereferenced its cash-flow column before checking there was one, which is a broken page where every sibling card returns a sentence. Five tests pin the four, and the boundary scan is the method rather than a one-off.

entries.title: The self-storage rate increase, and the runway it spends
entries.blurb: Storage leases month to month, so the operator can reprice a sitting tenant whenever it likes — the existing customer rate increase, eight to fifteen percent, once or twice a year. No other asset class can do it and every storage underwriting assumes it. The trade has a CLOSED FORM: raise the rate, some share move out, and the unit re-rents at the STREET rate, which on a mature facility is well below what the leaver was paying. On the seeded facility a 10% increase breaks even at a 25.8% move-out, against the three to eight percent an operator actually sees — 20.8 points of room, $53,501 of revenue and $837,410 of value. The reach cancels out of the break-even entirely: raising half the book and raising all of it break even at the same rate. Two more things the rent roll does not say. The ECRI EATS ITS OWN RUNWAY: each increase widens the gap the next one is traded against, so the break-even falls 25.8% to 20.7% over five years — and how fast is a race with the street rate's own growth, run rather than claimed. And the street rate and the in-place average are two different numbers: every tenant churned to today's ask earns $210,600 less, which on a facility about to face a new competitor is a forecast rather than a stress test.

entries.title: Taking over the seller's loan
entries.blurb: A broker marketing an assumable loan quotes the rate. The rate is not the answer. The seller's loan has been amortising for years and the building has appreciated since, so the balance is well under what a new loan would advance — assuming it is the LARGER cheque, not the smaller one: $2,376,000 more equity against $333,460 a year of saved debt service on the seeded $20M deal. Neither figure answers it, so the card runs BOTH COMPLETE POSITIONS and reports the two levered returns, then SOLVES the number to negotiate with — $934,223 of price, 4.7%, bisected rather than approximated, and a seller who does not ask for it hands it over. Two more things the flyer does not say. You are buying the OVERLAP, not the term: the premium is the same at five years remaining, seven and ten, because the building is sold at five either way. And the assumption buys COVERAGE as well as rate — 1.91x against 1.21x, which survives a coupon at today's market and no IRR shows it, so a marginal deal can be financeable one way only. A wonderful rate on a small balance, meanwhile, is worth almost nothing: $4M at 3.00% saves more debt service than the seed and prices at a tenth as much.

entries.title: What a hotel actually earns
entries.blurb: Forty-two cards and not one of them spoke a hotel's language. A hotel is the asset class whose lease is one night long, and three things follow. RevPAR is ONE number made of TWO levers that are not interchangeable: 10% more rate and 10% more occupancy are the same RevPAR and the same top line, and a different bottom line, because an occupied room costs money to turn and an empty one does not — $490,000 of value apart on the seeded hotel. The usual conclusion that rate always wins is wrong in one direction: occupancy brings ancillary spend and rate does not, so the card SOLVES the crossing, and it is not the obvious one — $32 of housekeeping needs $34.41 of ancillary revenue, because the management fee and the reserve are struck on that revenue and not on the cost of earning it. The penetration index is taken APART: the seeded hotel takes 90% of its fair share while charging 9% MORE than its competitive set, so the whole shortfall is empty rooms and cutting rate to chase the index would give away the one thing working. And the FF&E reserve is 4% of REVENUE, not of NOI — real cash a franchise agreement requires, and an 8.00% cap quoted before it is a 9.25% cap, $3.5M of price.

entries.title: The renovation program, and the part of the premium that is not renovation
entries.blurb: Page 12 of every multifamily memorandum quotes the value-add as one multiplication: $15,000 a door times 200 doors, $250 a month times 200 times twelve, "a twenty percent return on cost". Four things are wrong with that and they do not point the same way. The quoted premium is TWO numbers — the renovated comparable's rent less the subject's decomposes exactly into what renovation buys ($150) and the gap to a better building ($100), which granite does not close, so 40% of the value-add is the comparable being a different property. Turnover sets the pace, not ambition: at 35% the program runs 2.9 years against the two claimed, which would need half the book turning every year. The make-ready was owed at the turn whatever happened so it comes OUT of the cost, while the extra weeks the unit sits down are a real loss the invoice never mentioned — two corrections running opposite ways, which is why neither is ever made. Corrected, the 20% on cost is 13.4% and the $9.0M of value created is $4.5M. And the return on cost has no clock in it: the same program earns 63.7% sold the year it finishes and 31.4% held to a five-year exit, because 90% of its value is the resale rather than the rent. A renovation is a transaction, not an income strategy.

entries.title: The rent a new building needs
entries.blurb: "We are buying at sixty percent of replacement cost" is the most quoted comfort in the business, and on its own it protects nothing. Replacement cost says what it would cost to build. It says nothing about whether anyone WILL. The number that decides that is the feasibility rent — the rent a developer must underwrite to earn their required yield on cost — and it is a cost-side figure that can sit far above the rents actually being signed for years. On the seeded site a new building needs $42.08 a foot; the market signs $38.00, which is 3.5 years of growth away, and that gap is what keeps a competitor off the block. Raise the market rent to $52 and the same building, still bought at 53.3% of replacement cost, is exposed: the market already pays $9.92 a foot MORE than a new building needs, so the discount buys no protection from the one going up next door. The mirror is just as true — a building bought at 86% of replacement in a market 40% below feasibility has eleven years. Two more things the card says. Replacement cost carries today's LAND price, so the same building is a different percentage of it in two different years with no brick having moved. And the gap closes from either side: today's $38 already pencils at a hard cost of $263.37 against the $310 assumed, and the cost side is the one nobody models.

entries.title: What the statement reports, and what the building collects
entries.blurb: A seller's financials are prepared under GAAP, and GAAP does not report the rent a tenant paid this year. It reports the term's total rent divided by the term — the same figure every year, whatever the lease actually billed. So "NOI" read off an audited statement is deliberately not cash, and nothing on the page says so, because to an accountant it is not a discrepancy at all. On an escalating lease the difference is large, and the part people miss is that IT REVERSES. The seeded lease — 20,000 SF at $32 with 3% bumps and six months free — reports $701,688 of rent in year one against $320,000 actually collected, a gap of 119%. By year five cash overtakes it, and by year ten the statement UNDERSTATES the building by $133,367. So a rule of thumb like "knock ten percent off for straight-lining" is wrong half the time, in the wrong direction. Free rent is averaged in too, which is why the statement shows revenue in months the landlord banks nothing. The gap capitalises: $42,488 in year two, at a 6.5% cap, is $653,662 of price. And the deferred rent receivable it builds — $424,177 here — is the seller's asset, written off at closing, not something the buyer acquires. The identity underneath all of it: straight-line accounting moves rent between years and never creates any, so the cumulative gap returns to exactly zero at expiry.

entries.title: What the site actually holds
entries.blurb: Every development pro forma opens with a unit count, and that count almost always comes from ONE line of the zoning code — usually the density limit, because it is the one written as a number of units. The code imposes four at once and the site gets the smallest, so the number at the top of the model is an upper bound on an upper bound with nothing saying which line produced it. On the seeded two-acre site: density allows 160, floor area 198, height 238, and parking 140. Parking binds, and nobody writes that down. Two more traps. Floor area ratio is measured on GROSS building area and units are sold NET, so a 900 square foot apartment in an 82%-efficient building consumes 1,098 square feet of it — dividing buildable area by the unit size claims 242 units where the code allows 198, forty-four that are not there. And surface parking is not a separate cap at all: the spaces and the footprint compete for the same dirt, so the two are solved together. Switch to a deck and the site holds 160 instead of 140 — structured parking buys twenty units. Finally, a density bonus is a trade with an exact break-even: the set-aside is struck against the BONUSED count, so on these rents a 20% set-aside needs a bonus above 8.7% before it pays anything, and a 5% bonus for a 20% set-aside costs $150,000 a year while reading as free density.

entries.title: What the LP actually nets
entries.blurb: The IRR on the front of a syndication's deck is the PROPERTY's return — not the return any investor in that offering receives. The gap is two numbers from two causes that behave in opposite ways: the promote, which the sponsor earns only if the deal performs, and the fees, which it collects either way. A screening tool that models only the waterfall sees the first and is blind to the second, which is backwards — the promote gets its own page in every deck and the fees are three lines in the back with no arithmetic attached. On the seeded deal a 20.63% property return reaches the LP as 15.71%: 3.24 points of promote and 1.68 points of fees. A "1.5% acquisition fee" is 4.11% of the cheque the LP actually wires, because it is quoted against a price three times the size of the equity. A "1.5% asset management fee" is $164,250 a year on invested equity and $54,000 on gross revenue — $110,250 apart, on one word most term sheets leave out. And the fees sit ahead of the preferred return, so run the same deal weak and the promote is exactly zero while $1,581,250 of fees is still paid in full. That is why the card draws the sponsor's take twice: as underwritten it is 47.6% fees, and on an exit 10% softer it is 66.5%.

entries.title: What insurance really costs
entries.blurb: The expense line that reprices hardest and gets read least. The premium in a memorandum is the SELLER's expiring policy — bound on limits the seller chose, in a market that may no longer exist. Nothing in it is false; it is describing someone else's placement, which is exactly what makes it invisible. On the seeded Florida apartment the memorandum carries $420,000 and the quote comes back $780,000, and insurance is a fixed expense, so the whole $360,000 comes out of NOI: the advertised 5.25% cap is 4.60% to the buyer, or $6,857,143 of price. Then the figure nobody writes down. A named-storm deductible is a percentage of the INSURED VALUE, not a dollar amount — 5% of a $52M replacement cost is $2,600,000 retained per event, which is nine tenths of a year's NOI before the policy pays anything. The premium is the number people argue about; that is the number that takes the building.

entries.title: The sale-leaseback
entries.blurb: A company sells the building it operates from and signs a lease back the same day. Both sides then price it wrong in the same direction. The seller writes its own lease, so the rent is the price lever — a $9 contract rent on space letting at $7.50 turns a $21.6M building into a $27M price, and $5.4M of that is the lease rather than the real estate. It is cash borrowed, not value created. And an above-market lease reverts: the buyer is really buying the term's rent plus a market-rent building afterwards, which come to $23.0M — so capitalising the contract NOI overpays by $3,973,557, and it is worse on a SHORT lease, because the reversion arrives sooner. For the seller it is borrowing, and it looks cheaper than a mortgage without being cheaper: 6.09 cents a dollar against a 6.50% coupon, true for exactly four years before the escalations pass it.

entries.title: Filling an empty building
entries.blurb: The months between a building delivering and filling up are where a development's money goes, and the pro forma covers them in a footnote. Three things nobody models: an empty building still pays its taxes; a signed lease is not a paying lease, so the seeded building is full at month 22 and paid in full at month 28; and the tenant allowance and the commission fall due at signing, ahead of the rent they buy. So the worst month is month 22 — the month it fills — not month one: $6,200,437 out, deep into a lease-up that is going well. And then the part that catches people out. Stress the absorption and the reserve looks BETTER: six months slower takes the worst month down to $5,674,789, because a slower pace spends the leasing capital slower. Anyone stress-testing slippage against the lease-up reserve concludes it is survivable and is measuring the wrong thing. The cost is time, and it only shows at a common date — at month 36 the plan is $3,465,450 out and the slipped case $4,158,892, which is 1.9 times what a 5% rent miss costs on the same building.

entries.title: When the income rolls
entries.blurb: Paste a rent roll and get the weighted average lease term the three ways a memorandum does not quote it. Weight by rent rather than by area — they are different numbers, and the longer one gets printed, because the long leases in a building are the cheap ones. The seeded flex building runs 7.0 years by area and 5.1 by rent, on the strength of one distribution tenant twelve years out at $8.50. A tenant's break option is an expiry: you cannot make them stay and a lender will not assume they will, so the term to bid on is 4.3, and the schedule puts the space in the year the tenant can leave rather than the year the lease ends. And an average hides a cliff — two rolls with the same 3.0-year term roll 20% and 60% of the income in their worst year, which only the schedule can see. Year 4 of the seeded roll owes $1,530,000 of leasing capital against $1,292,000 of rent rolling off it: a cheque larger than the income at risk, and none of it in the NOI.

entries.title: What you can pay
entries.blurb: Every other calculator here judges a price somebody else set. This one solves for it — the last thing an analyst does before picking up the phone, and the calculation people fudge hardest, because doing it properly is circular. A lower price means a smaller loan at the same loan-to-value, which changes both the cheque and the debt service, which changes the return, so the price cannot be scaled off a return at some other price. It is solved by bisection — the levered IRR falls as the price rises, so the root is exact — and then the whole stream is rebuilt at the answer and run back through the same IRR function the Excel export uses, which is the check the card prints beside the price. On the seeded deal, $1.65M of NOI held five years and sold at a 6.00% cap, an equity that wants 15% can pay $25.54M, a 6.46% going-in cap. Three things it gets right that a spreadsheet usually does not. Which lender test governs MOVES with the price: loan-to-value scales with the price and the coverage tests do not, so the card solves for the crossing — $26.77M here — and a bid sitting near it is a bid whose financing assumption is about to stop being true. The target is LEVERED, and this is the only card where that is right: the debt is modelled, so the number to type is what the equity actually wants. And the cheque is not the price less the loan — closing costs and the loan fee are funded at closing, so they are equity at risk, and leaving them out overstates the bid by most of a million dollars.

entries.title: What sits below the NOI line
entries.blurb: A broker's NOI and an owner's NOI are different numbers for the same building, and the difference is not a disagreement about operations — it is a disagreement about what counts as an operating expense. Three things get pushed below the line on a marketing package: the replacement reserve, the tenant improvement allowance and the leasing commission. All three are real, recurring, unavoidable cash. A lender underwrites after them; so does a buyer who intends to own the building. The cover page does not. On the seeded 200,000-foot office building offered at $48M, they come to $308,800 a year, and the advertised 5.50% cap is 4.86% to the buyer — 64 basis points, or $5,614,545 of price, which is also exactly the difference between the $48M ask and the $42.39M at which the real NOI earns the advertised cap. Two rules make it honest. Capital that recurs is an expense: replacing a twenty-fifth of a roof every year forever is a cost of doing business, whatever an accountant calls it. And leasing capital is not optional, nor is its annual cost its invoice — a building on five-year leases re-tenants a fifth of itself a year, so spending nothing this year means the cost is late rather than absent. The largest line is also the least certain: at $144,000 if every rolling tenant renews and $472,000 if none does, a 3.3× range driven by nothing but an assumption, which the card draws as a range with the blend marked on it rather than printing one figure and hoping.

entries.title: Hold it or sell it
entries.blurb: The question every owner eventually asks, answered almost everywhere with the wrong number. A deal's lifetime IRR is an average over the whole hold and it is dominated by what already happened — the year the market re-rated, the year the renovation landed. It says nothing about next year, and a building can be sitting at a 17% lifetime IRR while the next twelve months earn six. This card runs the decision the right way round: the return on holding for ONE more year, on the cheque you could take out today. The seeded $34M building with $18.5M of debt has $14.82M of equity in it; holding one more year earns 14.1% on that, and the decay crosses a 12.5% reinvestment rate in year five — so the answer is a year, not a verdict. The decay is the point, and it is drawn: 14.1% falling to 11.0% over ten years with nothing going wrong, because the cash flow grows with rents while the equity underneath it grows faster, the loan amortising and the value rising on top. Two other rules earn their place. The capital at stake is the net sale proceeds — not the building's value, which ignores the debt, and not what you put in, which ignores that the market moved. And the cost of selling is paid whenever you sell, so it belongs on both sides: charge it against the hold year, the commonest version of this arithmetic, and the same year reads 18.8% instead of 14.1%, which on a 12.5% hurdle reverses the answer from "sell in five years" to "hold indefinitely".

entries.title: The doors against the dollars
entries.blurb: "95% occupied" is a count of doors. It is on the front of almost every multifamily memorandum, and it is the higher of the two numbers that could go there. The other one — what share of market rent the building actually banks — is routinely six or eight points lower, and every figure downstream of the NOI moves with it. This card walks the bridge a rent roll has to cross to become an operating statement. The seeded 200-unit building at $1,850 is 95% leased and collects 87.3% of market: three model units that are physically full and pay nothing, sitting tenants under market, concessions, and bad debt. Underwrite the cover page — vacancy off the top and nothing else — and the going-in cap reads 4.96% against an honest 4.30%, which at the cap this NOI really supports is $7,950,698 of price. Four rules make it honest. The denominator is market rent, never the in-place rent roll: divide by the rents currently charged and loss to lease vanishes into the denominator, and the same building reads 90.5%. Loss to lease is not a collections problem — it closes as leases roll rather than by managing anything — so the card says which bucket the largest part of the gap is in, because the buckets carry opposite instructions. A concession is rent you agreed not to collect and bad debt is rent you failed to. And other income stays out of the ratio: put the parking and the fees in the numerator and a full building prints above 100%.

entries.title: Which trailing window the memorandum chose
entries.blurb: Every offering memorandum quotes a trailing figure, and every one of them picks which trailing figure. "T-3 annualized" and "T-12" are both true statements about the same building; they are different numbers, and the seller quotes whichever is larger. Nothing on the cover page says a choice was made, which is what makes this the hardest trap on a summary page to see — there is no error to catch, only a selection. Paste the monthly column and this card runs all four windows at once and prices the choice: on the seeded building T-3 annualized reads $1,720,000 against a T-12 of $1,582,000, and that $138,000 at the stated 5.5% cap is $2,509,091 of value riding on which window the cover quoted. Then it does the thing a memorandum quoting T-3 almost never does — checks the last three months against the same three months a year earlier, where the season sits on both sides and cancels. The building really is growing, by 3.6%. The other five points were the summer. On an expense column the whole thing runs backwards, because there the seller wants the smallest figure and gets it by choosing a quarter that missed the tax bill: the card finds the lump, says which month it is, and names the windows that step over it.

entries.title: The interest reserve, run instead of guessed
entries.blurb: A construction loan funds its own interest, which makes the reserve circular — the loan pays interest on a balance that already contains the interest it has paid. A closed form needs an assumption about the shape of the draw, so every screening model in the business swaps the schedule for a constant, and this one did too: 0.55 of the loan outstanding on average, "an S-curve draw averages a little over half". This card runs the months instead, and the first thing it reports is how far that constant is off. On the seeded $30M project at 65% loan-to-cost the schedule says $1,357,269 and the shortcut says $1,905,738 — 40% high. The reason is a rule the constant does not know about: the lender requires the sponsor's equity fully funded first, so on a 65% loan the first seven of twenty-four months never touch the loan and the average outstanding is 42% of it, not 55%. Run the same project pari passu and the constant is roughly right, which is the point — it describes a funding order construction lenders do not actually use. And the error is the flattering kind to miss: an overstated reserve overstates cost and understates yield on cost, so it reads as prudence rather than as a mistake, and the deal it kills is killed quietly.

entries.title: Today's rates, and the loan they price
entries.blurb: The site has pulled the 10-year Treasury, SOFR, the 30-year mortgage survey and the CRE delinquency rate off FRED every weekday for months. They are now across the top of the calculators, each with the date of the observation behind it and a link to its series — and one of them fills a field. Which one is the point. A floating-rate note references SOFR by name, so today's SOFR IS the index on the new bridge-loan card, no adjustment and no term to match. The 10-year is shown and deliberately not used: yield maintenance prices at the Treasury matched to the REMAINING term, which on a normal curve sits lower, and a lower rate makes the penalty bigger — so reaching for the 10-year would understate what getting out costs. The mortgage survey is a residential owner-occupier rate and never fills a box at all. And stale is judged per series, because the quarterly delinquency figure is five months old when it is brand new: one threshold for all four would report three working feeds as broken.

entries.title: Whether the rate cap protects anything
entries.blurb: Every other debt tool here assumes a fixed rate; most of what gets screened in this market is a bridge loan floating over SOFR with a cap the lender required. The question nobody asks is whether that cap reaches far enough. The borrower buys the cheapest strike that satisfies the requirement — and on the seeded $20M at SOFR + 300, the 4.00% strike sits 8 basis points ABOVE the index level at which the loan breaks its own 1.20x covenant, which is at 3.92%. So rates rise, the loan fails, the lender takes the building, and only later does the cap begin to pay. It was protecting the lender the whole time. Today, the breach and the strike are drawn on one track so which comes first is visible before it is read. Three more things it says: the $300,000 premium is 75 bps a year, which is the only unit in which it can be set against a fixed quote; a floor is given away while a cap is bought, so the band runs 6.00% to 7.00% and is nowhere near centred on today; and the extension's cap has to be struck wherever the lender's test lands on the then-current NOI, which is the figure that kills deals.

entries.title: What it costs to get out of the loan early
entries.blurb: The calculation that decides whether a deal can be sold at all, and the one where the answer reverses on a fact about the market rather than about the building. Yield maintenance makes the lender whole on interest it will not now receive — so it is CHEAP when rates have risen (the lender can reinvest at more than your coupon, loses nothing, and the penalty drops to its 1% floor) and dear when they have fallen. On the seeded $20M at 3.75% with the matching Treasury at 4.75%, yield maintenance is $200,000 of pure floor. Defeasance is not a penalty at all but a purchase: you buy Treasuries that replicate the remaining payments, and when rates have risen that portfolio costs LESS than the balance it retires — here $460,213 less, a gain of $385,213 even after $75,000 of hard costs. So defeasance beats a penalty that can never go below its floor, and in a fallen-rate world the order reverses. The same move that makes the loan cheap to retire makes it $1,238,275 below market to a buyer who could assume it: both are worth having, only one can be had. And the open window costs nothing — the penalty is really the price of closing sooner, said here as a rate per month of waiting bought back.

entries.title: A below-market lease, and what it is worth to end
entries.blurb: The most common asset-management question, answered with the wrong arithmetic in both directions at once. The turnover — downtime, allowance, commission — is owed either way, so charging it against a buyout counts a cost you were always going to pay; and ending the lease does not hand you market rent tomorrow, it hands you the vacancy first. So the answer is the difference between two whole cash-flow streams, not a spread. On 40,000 feet at $28 against a $42 market the spread says $2.93M and the honest figure is $1.50M. Drop the in-place rent to $38 and the answer flips sign: the spread says pay $908,072 to end it, the streams say pay them $527,092 to stay. Two consequences the card draws: a lease with nothing left to run is worth nothing to end, however far under market, because the spread is still there on the last day; and the spread cancels between landlord and tenant, so with no frictions and one discount rate there is exactly zero on the table. What makes a buyout happen is vacant possession being worth something the rent does not contain, or a tenant who discounts the future far harder than you do.

entries.title: The blend is hiding it
entries.blurb: The layers between the senior loan and the cheque — the mezzanine and preferred most deals actually get done with. Leverage is tested layer by layer, never on the average: a $100M stack blends to 6.13% against a 6.5% yield on cost, which reads fine, and both layers above the senior cost more than the building earns. A big cheap senior drags the average under the line while the expensive layers take from the equity. Amortisation is a transfer, not a cost, so the rate decides whether a layer earns its place and the constant sizes the coverage. An accruing preferred flatters the current return by removing equity while paying nothing: this stack takes $900,000 a year out of cash flow and cash-on-cash still rises, 6.59% to 7.89%, with $13.48M owed at the sale and $1.08M of that the compounding alone. Three coverage ratios, not one: 1.68x on the senior, 1.36x once the mezzanine counts — the ratio that decides who can take the property.

entries.title: What you would have to believe
entries.blurb: Every other calculation on the deal math page takes assumptions and gives you a number. This one runs backwards. You give it the price and the return you need, and it tells you the NOI growth rate the deal is quietly assuming — the most useful sanity check in screening, because a pro forma is a set of assumptions chosen to reach a conclusion, and a deal that pencils at 3% growth and one that pencils at 9% look identical on a summary page. The seeded example is an ordinary one: $25M for $1.5M of NOI, a 6.00% going-in cap, held five years and sold at 6.25%. Ask it for 12% unlevered and it needs NOI to grow 7.16% a year, every year, for five years. That is 4.16 points past the 3% you would probably call ordinary, and the card says so in a word rather than leaving you to do the subtraction. The same deal can be made to work the other way, so it solves that lever too: leave growth at ordinary and the exit cap has to come in to 5.01% — 99 basis points TIGHTER than the cap you are buying at. That is worth naming plainly, because it is a bet on the market re-rating rather than on the building earning more, and it is the assumption most likely to be buried in a model instead of argued for. Two things it is careful about. The exit capitalises next year’s NOI rather than this year’s, because that is what the next buyer is purchasing — using the trailing year understates every exit by a full year of growth. And the required rate is solved rather than searched for, then checked: a test rebuilds the cash flow at the solved rate and runs it through the same IRR function that sits behind the Excel export, so the page and the workbook can never drift apart. One caveat the card states in as many words: this return is unlevered. Most stated targets are not. A 12% levered on 60% debt is a far smaller ask than a 12% unlevered one, and a levered number typed in here will make any deal look heroic.

entries.title: A building on someone else’s land
entries.blurb: The ground lease now has its own calculation, and it is the one structure where the ordinary screening arithmetic is not slightly off but wrong by a multiple — in the flattering direction. A leasehold is a wasting asset. When the lease ends the building goes back to the landowner and the leasehold is worth nothing, so its value is the present value of the cash flows over the years that remain and nothing after them. Capitalise its NOI at a fee-simple cap, which is what a screening model does unless told otherwise, and you have valued a perpetuity that expires. On the seeded lease — $8M of NOI, $2M of ground rent, forty years left — that shortcut says $120M and the honest answer is $97.5M. The page draws both bars so the gap is visible rather than argued. And the gap grows as the clock runs: the same lease with ten years left is 62.8% imaginary. Underneath it, the number a ground-lease lender actually underwrites, which is not the DSCR. On an unsubordinated lease the ground rent sits ahead of the mortgage — miss it and the landlord can terminate the lease, which takes the building and the mortgage with it — so the test is how many times the NOI covers the ground rent. This one covers four times today. It covers 2.22 times after the reset, because the rent resets to a percentage of land value rather than stepping by a fixed escalation, and nothing in the lease caps that. If land doubles, coverage falls to 1.11. The card also says whether the thing is financeable at all: an unsubordinated lease has to outlast the loan by a wide margin or no lender will look at it. Last, the other half of the same lease. The landlord holds the rent plus the land coming back, which is closer to a bond than a building — and it moves the opposite way as the term shortens, because the clock that destroys the leasehold is the clock that returns the land sooner. Two halves of one asset, priced from opposite ends of the same lease. That is why they trade to different buyers.

entries.title: The tax bill in the memorandum is the seller’s
entries.blurb: A new calculation on the deal math page, for the error that hides in plain sight. Every offering memorandum shows property taxes in the expense line, and in much of the country that figure is struck on an assessed value set when the SELLER bought — which has drifted ever since under a cap, a phase-in, or an assessor who simply has not looked. Where the jurisdiction reassesses on transfer, your purchase resets the assessment to what you paid. Nothing in the memorandum is false. It is describing someone else’s ownership, and it stops being true the day after closing. On the seeded deal — an ordinary $25M building the seller has held long enough for the assessment to fall to $14M — the bill goes from $210,000 to $375,000, and the 6.00% cap on the cover is 5.34% to the buyer. Sixty-six basis points, on figures that all tie. The page says it twice, because the two audiences are different: as a cap, which is what people quote to each other, and as a price, which is what they negotiate with. That price is solved rather than estimated: paying less lowers the assessment, which lowers the tax, which raises the NOI, so the answer feeds back on itself. Here it is $22.8M — $2.2M below the ask, and $550,000 more than the tempting shortcut of capitalising the lower NOI would have told you. Three more things it insists on. A tax bill is assessed value times a rate, and assessed value is usually not the price, so the ratio is a separate field; where you give it both the current bill and the current assessment it works out what rate is really being charged and tells you when that disagrees with what you typed. A phase-in is a deferral, not a discount — year one is shown, and the stabilized bill is the headline, because that is the one that prices the exit. And a jurisdiction that does not reassess gets a real answer rather than a blank. Which ones do is a fact about a place, not arithmetic, so the card asks you and says to check the county.

entries.title: The loan schedule leaves the page as numbers
entries.blurb: Run a loan over its hold on the deal math page and you get a row per year — opening balance, interest, principal, debt service, closing balance, and whether that year was interest-only. Useful to look at, and until now the one table there you had to retype to use. It has a Copy button now, the same one the cash flow strip has had: tab-delimited with a header row and the numbers raw, no dollar signs and no commas, so it pastes into a spreadsheet as numbers rather than as text you then have to clean a column at a time. The interest-only years come across as a plain Yes/No column, because a balance that sits flat for two years reads as a broken schedule unless something says why. Small companion fix while we were here: copy buttons no longer print. They were showing up on paper as little empty boxes — a button nobody can click on a sheet of paper is just ink.

entries.title: Percentage rent, and the breakpoint nobody checks
entries.blurb: The retail lease's own arithmetic, and it opens on a year that owes nothing and still gets billed. The natural breakpoint is not negotiated — it is the base rent divided by the percentage rate, the sales level at which the two would be equal, $2.00M on the seeded lease. Anything else a lease states is an artificial breakpoint, which is a normal thing to negotiate and an easy thing to read past, so the page derives the natural one always and says which side an artificial one favours. Then the part that costs money. Percentage rent is owed on the YEAR'S sales and reconciled at year end. Bill it monthly against a twelfth of the breakpoint with no true-up and the landlord collects on every strong month while refunding nothing for the weak ones — so this seasonal tenant, whose year lands under the breakpoint and owes nothing, pays $22,300. Two months of Christmas clear the line and the ten months below it give nothing back. No single month's statement shows that, which is why the card draws all twelve with the line across them. Underneath, the occupancy cost ratio — base plus percentage plus CAM, taxes and insurance, over sales — because a rent the tenant cannot carry gets renegotiated whatever the lease says. It solves for the sales that would reach whatever ceiling you set, and tells you when there is no such figure: a 5% ceiling on a 6% lease can never be reached, and printing a number there would be a lie.

entries.title: The pictures survive the printer
entries.blurb: Almost everything this site draws is made of background colour — a debt sizer's three tests, a cash flow's years, a gain split into the rates it is taxed at, a comp's basis against the subject. Browsers throw background colours away when they print, because "Background graphics" is a checkbox nobody ticks. So printing the deal math page, or saving it as a PDF to put in a file, gave you nineteen cards of empty grey tracks with the figures floating above them. Fixed, and measured rather than assumed: the same page printed the same way was dropping just under two kilobytes of colour, and now drops none. The page also knows what paper does not want. The photograph at the top comes off — it is a page of ink for no information, and the dark band keeps its heading without it. So do the site's own header, footer, the jump index and the copy-link button, none of which can be clicked on a sheet of paper. And a card never splits across two pages, because a bar on one sheet and its figure on the next is worse than a short page.

entries.title: What the tenant actually owes
entries.blurb: The operating-expense reconciliation that lands every spring and that almost nobody checks — with the move that costs the most money drawn rather than described. Variable expenses scale with occupancy, so a base year struck while the building was 72% leased is artificially low, and a tenant who does not catch it ends up paying its share of the building filling up. The protection is to gross BOTH years up to the same occupancy: on the seeded building that adds $287,500 to the base year and $12,553 to this one, which is why the two bars sit side by side with the adjustment shaded on the end. Do it to only the current year — the commonest error in a reconciliation, and the one hardest to see — and this tenant is billed $38,623 instead of $10,206. The cap catches part of that and no more, which is the honest thing to say about a cap: it is a backstop against an error, never a substitute for finding one. Three more rules it holds to. A base year is an outcome and can drift; an expense stop is a negotiated number and cannot. A cumulative cap banks the headroom a quiet year did not use and a non-cumulative one loses it, though a term sheet calls both "a 5% cap". And a cap reaches controllable expenses only, so in a year the insurance jumps it is worth far less than it sounds. The answer is a direction, not a total: on these figures the tenant is owed $19,794 back.

entries.title: What a 1031 exchange actually defers
entries.blurb: The card above it prices the tax bill at a sale. This one answers what happens if you roll the gain into the next deal instead — and it opens on a trade that looks completely sensible and still owes $305,000. Sell for $26M, buy for $30M with more debt on it, and the price test passes comfortably; $1.22M of proceeds stayed in your pocket, and nothing about borrowing more on the other side cures that. Debt runs the other way: coming down on the mortgage is taxable even when every dollar of cash is reinvested, but cash you add to the replacement offsets it. So the page draws three tests rather than one, and names the one that binds. Two more things it says out loud. The bill on boot is filled depreciation-first, at the higher rate, so the first dollars out are the expensive ones.
